name: Iguazú Falls
scope: A chain of waterfalls in the subtropical jungle on the Iguazú River, straddling the Brazil (Paraná)–Argentina (Misiones) border just above where it joins the Paraná. T1: it isn't ONE waterfall but a system of up to 275 separate cascades strung in a 2.7-km arc (the number is the hook; answer = a system of hundreds of falls). T2: the biggest, most violent gullet — a U-shaped chasm where 14 cataracts converge and plunge ~80 m — has a devilish name (answer = the Devil's Throat / Garganta del Diablo). T3: the Guaraní who lived here gave the river its name, which simply means 'big water'; oral legend says a forest deity sliced the river in fury when a girl fled with her lover (answer = Iguazú means 'big water' in Guaraní; the legend is labeled as legend). T4: the whole river tumbles off the edge of a vast ancient lava sheet — the hard black rock is flood basalt of the Paraná Plateau (answer = a flood-basalt plateau; teach 'flood basalt'). T5: like Niagara, the falls are slowly sawing themselves UPSTREAM — the soft rock beneath the basalt caprock washes out and the ledge collapses backward (answer = headward erosion / the falls retreat upstream). Extra rung: the arc is roughly three times wider than Niagara — Eleanor Roosevelt is said to have gasped 'Poor Niagara!' (hook = the comparison; answer = Iguazú is far wider).
source: Wikipedia 'Iguazu Falls' & 'Devil's Throat, Iguazu Falls'; Britannica 'Garganta del Diablo'; corroborated cataract count (150–300 seasonal, ~275 typical), 82 m Devil's Throat, Paraná Plateau basalt. Grokipedia page exists (fetch blocked 403).
framing_note: Pure place→wonder voice: every rung a different marvel of THIS one falls-system, scene-led (a curtain of jungle water), never 'What is the largest waterfall?'. Accuracy rail: give the SEASONAL cataract range (150–300, ~275 typical) not a false-precise single count, and LABEL the Guaraní serpent-god story as legend/oral tradition, not fact. Dinner-test payoff = the Devil's Throat (14 falls into one throat). Lane border: the great dusky swifts that nest behind the water curtain are an ANIMAL-bank aside — keep any such answer the PLACE feature (the ledges behind the falls), never the bird's biology; a Guaraní-dish mention is fine but no food-origin rung.

name: Niagara Falls
scope: Three falls on the Niagara River between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, on the Ontario (Canada)–New York (USA) border. T1: of the three, the great curved one that carries ~90% of the water is shaped like a horseshoe (answer = the Horseshoe Falls). T2: the falls are marching UPSTREAM — over the ~12,000 years since the Ice Age they have eaten ~11 km backward from the cliff where they began (answer = they retreat/erode upstream; hook = a moving waterfall). T3: WHY they erode — a hard cap of dolostone sits on soft shale; the river scoops out the shale until the unsupported ledge breaks off (answer = a hard caprock undercut by soft shale; teach 'caprock/knickpoint'). T4: in late March 1848 the falls briefly went SILENT — an ice jam plugged the river at Lake Erie and people walked on the dry riverbed (answer = an ice jam stopped the falls, 1848). T5: the whole waterfall was BORN when retreating Ice-Age glaciers let the Great Lakes drain over a long ridge (answer = the retreating glaciers / meltwater over the Niagara Escarpment; teach 'escarpment'). Extra rungs: downstream the gorge makes a right-angle turn into the violent rotating Whirlpool basin; engineers twice 'shut off' the American Falls (1969) to study the crumbling rock.
source: Wikipedia & Britannica 'Niagara Falls'; International Joint Commission 'Niagara Falls is Moving'; NY State Museum. Corroborated ~11 km / 12,000-yr retreat, Lockport dolomite over Rochester shale, 1848 ice-jam stoppage. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: the wonder is that a waterfall MOVES and once fell silent — scene-led, never 'What is the erosion rate of Niagara?'. Accuracy rail: today's regulated retreat is far slower (~0.3 m/yr or less) than the historic ~1 m/yr — don't quote the old fast rate as current. Dinner-test payoff = the 1848 day the falls went dry. Lane border: hydro-power / Tesla belongs to history/tech — keep every rung on the river, the caprock, and the Ice-Age origin.

name: Victoria Falls
scope: A curtain of the Zambezi River on the Zambia–Zimbabwe border. T1: the spray plume is visible from 30+ km away; the people who lived here called it 'the smoke that thunders' long before David Livingstone renamed it for his queen in 1855 (answer = Mosi-oa-Tunya; the indigenous name is the answer). T2: at 108 m tall and 1,708 m wide it is neither the tallest nor the widest waterfall, yet it is called the greatest — because it forms the largest single SHEET of falling water on Earth (invert: the dimensions are the hook, 'largest sheet of falling water' the answer). T3: at the very lip, in the low-water months (Sep–Dec), a rock rim lets swimmers wade into a natural infinity pool at the edge of the 100-m drop (answer = the Devil's Pool). T4: below the falls the river doesn't run straight — it zigzags through a series of sharp gorges, and each gorge is a place the waterfall USED to be (answer = the gorges are seven former falls / former lips). T5: WHY the zigzag — the Zambezi pours over a flat basalt sheet criss-crossed by cracks; it tears the falls back along one crack, then jumps to the next (answer = cracks/fault lines in a basalt plateau). Extra rung: on full-moon nights the spray throws a rare 'moonbow' (lunar rainbow).
source: Wikipedia 'Victoria Falls'; UNESCO WHC #509 'Mosi-oa-Tunya'; Zambia Tourism. Corroborated 108 m × 1,708 m, Devil's Pool (Sep–Dec low water, Livingstone Island), zigzag gorges = seven former falls on basalt. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: story-led wonder — lead with the smoke-that-thunders you see before you hear it. Accuracy rail: name the indigenous 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' FIRST and frame Livingstone as the one who renamed it, not who 'discovered' a place people already knew; give the Devil's Pool season (low water only). Dinner-test payoff = the Devil's Pool at the very lip. Lane border: no food/animal rungs; the zigzag-gorge earth-process is the intellectual T4/T5 climb.

name: Angel Falls
scope: The world's tallest waterfall, in Canaima National Park, Venezuela, plunging off Auyán-tepui. T1: it drops so far — 979 m, the tallest on Earth — that on windy days the water breaks into MIST and blows away before it reaches the bottom (answer = the water atomizes into mist before landing; this is the dinner-test payoff). T2: it pours off the sheer edge of a flat-topped table mountain that rises straight out of the rainforest (answer = a tepui / Auyán-tepui; teach 'tepui'). T3: the Pemón people who live below it call it Kerepakupai Merú, 'waterfall of the deepest place'; its English name honors the American bush pilot Jimmie Angel, who flew over it in 1933 and crash-landed atop the tepui in 1937 (answer = Kerepakupai Merú, the Pemón name). T4: these isolated table-tops, with strange life marooned on their summits, so captured imaginations that Arthur Conan Doyle set a dinosaur-haunted 'Lost World' on one (answer = The Lost World — a cultural creation born of the place). T5: the tepuis are eroded stumps of an ancient sandstone plateau on the Guiana Shield, among the oldest exposed rock on Earth (answer = eroded remnants of an ancient sandstone plateau; teach the layered sandstone).
source: Wikipedia & Britannica 'Angel Falls'; geology.com highest-waterfall; Wondermondo. Corroborated 979 m total / 807 m plunge, Auyán-tepui, Pemón name Kerepakupai Merú, Jimmie Angel 1933/1937. Grokipedia not fetched (403).
framing_note: Voice: the wonder is a waterfall so tall the water becomes cloud — scene-led, never 'What is the tallest waterfall?'. Accuracy rail: credit the Pemón name and DON'T call Jimmie Angel the 'discoverer' of a place the Pemón already knew; note the falls feed tributaries of the Orinoco (via the Churún/Carrao). Dinner-test payoff = T1 (mist before it lands). Lane border: the carnivorous plants and endemic frogs marooned atop the tepui are an ANIMAL/biology aside — keep answers the PLACE (the tabletop isolation, the sandstone), not the species. Colonial-naming is handled in framing, not a contested-stance lever.

name: The Nile
scope: The world's longest river, in northeast Africa. T1: it does what rivers 'shouldn't' — it flows NORTH, from the heart of Africa to the Mediterranean (answer = it flows north; hook = longest river). T2: it has two branches that join at Sudan's capital — the clear one from the great lakes and the muddy one from the Ethiopian mountains (answer = the White Nile and Blue Nile meet at Khartoum). T3: almost all the water and nearly all the black silt that fed Egypt actually comes from ONE branch, off the Ethiopian highlands (answer = the Blue Nile, from Lake Tana; invert the White-is-longer assumption). T4: for millennia the river flooded every summer and left a strip of fertile black mud the Egyptians called kemet, 'the black land' (answer = the annual flood and silt / the black land — an earth-process that birthed a civilization). T5: between Aswan and Khartoum the river tumbles over six stretches of rapids where hard granite crosses the channel (answer = the cataracts; teach 'cataract'). Extra rungs: before the sea it fans into a broad triangular delta — the original 'delta,' named for the Greek letter Δ (answer = the Nile Delta, the shape that named 'delta'); its ultimate source is traced to Lake Victoria, though the farthest headwater stream is debated (answer = Lake Victoria; mark the source as long-disputed).
source: Wikipedia & Britannica 'Nile'; National Geographic. Corroborated north flow, White (Lake Victoria) + Blue (Lake Tana) meeting at Khartoum, ~90% of water/silt from Ethiopia (~59% Blue Nile alone), six cataracts, delta etymology. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: place→wonder — the river that runs the 'wrong' way and grew a civilization out of mud. Accuracy rail: the Blue Nile supplies MOST of the water (~59%) and the fertile silt, but the White Nile is the longer/steadier branch — don't conflate 'longer' with 'more water'; flag the ultimate-source question as genuinely disputed. Dinner-test payoff = T4 (the flood that made 'the black land') or the delta rung that names the very word 'delta'. Lane border: Ancient Egypt's pharaohs, pyramids, and dynasties belong to the HISTORY bank — keep every Nile rung on hydrology and landscape (north flow, silt, sources, cataracts, delta), not political history.
history_overlap: Ancient Egyptian civilization (pharaohs/dynasties/pyramids) is the history bank's territory; keep Nile rungs on the river's geography and flood-silt earth-process, not specific historical episodes.

name: The Amazon
scope: The mightiest river on Earth, crossing South America to the Atlantic. T1: one river carries about a FIFTH of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans — more than the next seven biggest rivers combined (answer = the Amazon, largest by discharge; the fifth-of-all-water is the hook). T2: at Manaus two rivers meet but refuse to blend — the coffee-dark Rio Negro and the sandy pale Rio Solimões run side by side in two colors for kilometers (answer = the Meeting of the Waters / Encontro das Águas; caused by different temperature, speed, and sediment). T3: twice a year the Atlantic tide shoves a wall of water up to 4 m high hundreds of kilometers UP the river — a roaring wave surfers ride for minutes (answer = the pororoca, a tidal bore; teach 'tidal bore'; dinner-test payoff). T4: despite being up to 20 km wide in flood season, the entire main river has not a single BRIDGE across it (answer = it has no bridges — soft shifting banks and few roads). T5: the river begins as a trickle high in the Peruvian Andes, only a short distance from the PACIFIC, then flows all the way east across the continent to the Atlantic (answer = it rises in the Andes, near the Pacific). Extra rung: the flood pushes so much fresh water out that a brownish plume dilutes the salty Atlantic more than 100 km offshore.
source: Wikipedia 'Amazon River' & 'Pororoca'; Britannica; Live Science 'Why no bridges over the Amazon'. Corroborated ~20% of global riverine discharge, Encontro das Águas at Manaus (~6 km unmixed), pororoca (4 m, ~800 km inland), no main-stem bridge, Andean source. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: superlative-as-hook, knowable-thing-as-answer — the fifth-of-all-water opens to 'largest by discharge,' never 'What is the biggest river?'. Accuracy rail: the Amazon is largest by VOLUME/discharge (the Nile is longest) — keep that distinction crisp; the Rio Negro/Manaus bridge crosses a tributary, not the Amazon's main stem, so 'no bridge' still holds. Dinner-test payoff = the pororoca. Lane border: the pink river dolphins and piranhas are ANIMAL-bank — keep answers the PLACE/hydrology (blackwater vs whitewater, the unmixed confluence), never the creatures' biology; no food-origin rung.

name: The Yangtze
scope: Asia's longest river, crossing China from Tibet to the East China Sea. T1: partway along, the river squeezes through three dramatic canyons of sheer cliffs (answer = the Three Gorges — Qutang, Wu, and Xiling). T2: spanning the river at the Xiling gorge stands the largest hydroelectric power station on the planet (answer = the Three Gorges Dam). T3: the reservoir behind it holds so much water raised so high that NASA scientists calculated it very slightly SLOWED Earth's spin, lengthening the day by a fraction of a microsecond (answer = it minutely slowed Earth's rotation; dinner-test payoff). T4: filling that reservoir drowned whole riverside cities and cliffs of ancient carved poetry and forced well over a million people to move (answer = it displaced more than a million people / drowned the old gorge towns). T5: the whole river is born from glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau, the 'roof of the world,' and crosses the width of China to the sea (answer = the Tibetan Plateau, its glacial source).
source: Wikipedia 'Three Gorges' & 'Three Gorges Dam'; Britannica 'Yangtze River'; NASA (B. F. Chao) day-length calculation (+0.06 µs). Corroborated Qutang/Wu/Xiling, world's largest power station, ~1.3 M displaced, Tibetan-Plateau source. Grokipedia not fetched (403).
framing_note: Voice: place→wonder — canyons so deep China built the world's biggest dam there. Accuracy rail: attribute the 'slowed Earth's rotation' fact to the actual NASA moment-of-inertia calculation (a real but truly tiny 0.06-microsecond effect) — don't inflate it into something a person could feel. Dinner-test payoff = T3 (the dam that nudged Earth's spin). Lane border: the now-extinct baiji river dolphin is ANIMAL-bank — keep the answer the PLACE (the gorges, the reservoir), not the animal.

name: The Mekong
scope: A great river of Southeast Asia, running from Tibet to the Vietnamese sea. T1: in Cambodia one river does the impossible — for half the year it flows one direction, then REVERSES and runs backward (answer = the Tonlé Sap, whose flow reverses twice a year; dinner-test payoff). T2: it reverses because the monsoon-swollen Mekong backs up and shoves water INTO a lake, swelling it nearly sixfold and drowning the forest floor (answer = the monsoon flood pulse pushes water up into Tonlé Sap lake). T3: in southern Laos the river shatters into thousands of channels around islands — a maze the locals call Si Phan Don, 'the 4,000 islands' (answer = Si Phan Don / the 4,000 Islands). T4: there the water crashes over the widest waterfall in the world, a barrier so wide it blocks boats from ever sailing up into China (answer = Khone Phapheng Falls, the world's widest waterfall). T5: the Mekong is born on the Tibetan Plateau and touches SIX countries before the sea — China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam (answer = it flows through six countries; hook = the Tibetan glacial source).
source: Wikipedia 'Khone Phapheng Falls' & 'Tonlé Sap'; NASA Earth Observatory 'Tonle Sap Wetlands'. Corroborated twice-yearly reversal & ~6× lake expansion (2,700→~16,000 km²), Si Phan Don, Khone Phapheng widest (~10.8 km), six-country course. Grokipedia pages exist for both (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: the river that runs backward and the waterfall too wide to cross — scene-led wonder. Accuracy rail: the Tonlé Sap reversal is driven by the monsoon flood pulse (not tides); keep 'widest waterfall' as by-WIDTH, not tallest. Dinner-test payoff = T1 (the river that reverses). Lane border: the Mekong giant catfish and the fisheries' fish are ANIMAL/economics territory — keep answers the PLACE and its hydrology.

name: The Ganges
scope: India's holiest river, running from the Himalaya to the Bay of Bengal. T1: it bursts out of an ice cave at the snout of a Himalayan glacier — a spot shaped like a cow's mouth (answer = Gaumukh, 'cow's mouth,' the snout of the Gangotri Glacier; teach 'glacier snout'). T2: Hindus revere the river as the goddess Ganga and believe bathing in it washes away sin; pilgrims gather by the millions on the stone steps at Varanasi (answer = it is sacred — the goddess Ganga — a cultural life centered on this place). T3: the river ends by joining the Brahmaputra and fanning into the largest river delta on Earth (answer = the Ganges–Brahmaputra Delta, the world's biggest delta). T4: that delta holds the largest mangrove forest on the planet, a tiger-haunted maze of tidal channels (answer = the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest). T5: sailors and scientists long noticed Ganges water seems to resist rotting; researchers credit natural viruses called bacteriophages carried from the glacier — a claim still debated (answer = bacteriophages / a self-purifying effect, LABELED as an observed-but-debated hypothesis).
source: Wikipedia & Britannica 'Ganges'; NASM/ASM microbiome studies on Ganga bacteriophages (peer-reviewed but contested). Corroborated Gaumukh/Gangotri source, Ganges–Brahmaputra largest delta, Sundarbans largest mangrove, self-purifying/phage hypothesis. Grokipedia not fetched (403).
framing_note: Voice: place→wonder — a river born in an ice cave, worshiped as a goddess, ending in the world's biggest delta. Accuracy rail: the 'self-cleaning Ganges' MUST be framed as observed-and-hypothesized (bacteriophages), NOT settled fact — the modern river is also heavily polluted; present the Hindu sacredness neutrally and respectfully as a cultural fact of the place. Dinner-test payoff = Gaumukh, the cow's-mouth ice cave, or the tiger-haunted Sundarbans. Lane border: the Bengal tiger and Ganges river dolphin are ANIMAL-bank — keep the Sundarbans answer the PLACE (mangrove delta), not the tiger.

name: The Mississippi
scope: America's great river, draining the continent's heart to the Gulf of Mexico. T1: it doesn't run straight — it loops and coils across its wide floodplain in giant S-bends (answer = meanders; teach 'meander'). T2: when a loop gets pinched off, it's left stranded beside the river as a crescent-shaped lake (answer = an oxbow lake; teach 'oxbow'). T3: where it finally reaches the Gulf, the river splits into a few long fingers of land poking into the sea, shaped like a bird's foot (answer = the bird's-foot delta). T4: the river and its tributaries drain an astonishing 41% of the lower 48 states — water from 31 states funnels down it (invert: the huge basin is the hook; answer = it drains ~40% of the continental U.S. / 31 states). T5: in the winter of 1811–12 the New Madrid earthquakes shook the valley so violently that eyewitnesses reported the river briefly appeared to run BACKWARD (answer = the New Madrid earthquakes made the river run backward, LABELED as reported/temporary; dinner-test payoff). Extra rung: for all its might it begins as a stream you can wade across, flowing out of little Lake Itasca in Minnesota (answer = Lake Itasca, its humble source).
source: Wikipedia 'Mississippi River'; NPS Mississippi River facts; USGS/NASA Earth Observatory 'Mississippi Meanders'. Corroborated meanders/oxbows, bird's-foot delta, 41% / 31 states / two provinces watershed, Lake Itasca source, 1811–12 New Madrid retrograde-flow reports. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: earth-process wonder a kid can picture — a river that draws loops, builds a bird's foot, and once flowed backward. Accuracy rail: the 'ran backward' claim is real eyewitness testimony from the New Madrid quakes (uplift + seismic seiche), TEMPORARY and local — label it as reported, not a permanent reversal. Dinner-test payoff = the earthquake that reversed the river, or the bird's-foot delta. Lane border: keep rungs on landform and hydrology (meander→oxbow→delta→watershed→source); riverboat/blues/steamboat culture is history/trivia territory.
history_overlap: If the history bank treats the 1811–12 New Madrid earthquakes as an American-history episode, keep the Mississippi rung on the river's retrograde-flow earth-process, not the settlement/frontier history.

name: The Congo
scope: A colossal river arcing across central Africa to the Atlantic. T1: in places it plunges to over 220 m deep — the DEEPEST river on Earth, deep enough to swallow a 70-story building (answer = the deepest river; the depth is the hook). T2: it is the only major river to cross the equator TWICE, so some part of its basin is always in a rainy season and the flow never runs dry (answer = it crosses the equator twice, giving year-round steady flow). T3: near the sea the whole river funnels into a narrow canyon and drops through a furious staircase of rapids — some of the most powerful whitewater on Earth (answer = the Livingstone Falls / Inga rapids; teach 'cataracts/rapids'). T4: it pours out more water than any river but the Amazon, draining a vast shallow interior basin like a giant bathtub (answer = second-largest river by discharge). T5: the river is so powerful it keeps carving even underwater — a deep submarine canyon runs ~800 km out across the Atlantic seafloor from its mouth (answer = the Congo submarine canyon; a hidden earth-process; dinner-test payoff).
source: Wikipedia 'Congo River'; Live Science 'Congo River deepest'; WorldAtlas. Corroborated ~220 m max depth (deepest), crosses equator twice, Livingstone Falls/Inga rapids, second-by-discharge, ~800 km Congo submarine canyon. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Voice: superlative-as-hook — the deepest, most powerful river, always raining somewhere along it. Accuracy rail: state the depth carefully (~220 m, world's deepest RIVER — not lake) and frame discharge as 'second only to the Amazon,' the standard claim. Dinner-test payoff = the underwater canyon reaching 800 km out to sea, or the deepest-river depth. Lane border: the deep rapids split fish into separate species — that speciation is ANIMAL-bank; keep the answer the PLACE (the deep, violent channel), not the fish.

name: The Yellow River (Huang He)
scope: China's second-longest river and the cradle of its civilization. T1: the whole river runs a muddy yellow-brown — it carries more silt than any river on Earth, and that mud gives it its name (answer = windblown yellow silt, called loess, colors it). T2: the silt comes from a vast plateau of soft, wind-piled dust the river slices through on its way down (answer = the Loess Plateau; teach 'loess'). T3: so much silt drops out on the flat lower river that the bed rises ABOVE the surrounding farmland — the river now flows overhead, held in only by man-made banks (answer = a 'suspended' or perched river; dinner-test payoff). T4: when those banks break, the floods are catastrophic — the river has drowned the plains so often it earned the grim nickname 'China's Sorrow' (answer = 'China's Sorrow'). T5: that same fertile yellow-earth floodplain was where Chinese civilization was born thousands of years ago (answer = the birthplace/cradle of Chinese civilization — an earth-process that grew a civilization).
source: Wikipedia & Britannica 'Yellow River / Huang He'; SCMP 'Why China's Yellow River is so yellow'; WorldAtlas 'China's Sorrow'. Corroborated most-sediment-laden river, Loess Plateau source, perched/suspended riverbed, 'China's Sorrow' floods, cradle of Chinese civilization. Grokipedia page exists (fetch 403).
framing_note: Strong canonical ADDITION beyond the seed list — a 'great river' set without the Huang He has a real gap. Voice: place→wonder — a river that runs yellow, floats above the land, and grew a civilization. Accuracy rail: the perched/'suspended' riverbed is a genuine, well-documented consequence of silt deposition — present it precisely (the bed rises above the plain behind levees), not as hyperbole. Dinner-test payoff = T3 (a river flowing above the rooftops). Lane border: dynastic Chinese history is the HISTORY bank — keep the 'cradle of civilization' rung on the geography (the loess soil/floodplain that made settlement possible), not specific dynasties or emperors.
history_overlap: Chinese dynastic history belongs to the history bank; keep the Yellow River rungs on the physical geography (loess, silt, perched channel, floods) and frame the 'cradle of civilization' rung as the earth-process/soil that enabled it, not as a history episode.
